basis: Written from the published specification and established practice in the field; no new sources were read. Unreviewed.

distinguishingFeatures: Holds the scheme and its concepts, not the assignment of concepts to objects, which is the classification binding model.
A concept has a stable identifier; labels and codes are names for it and may change or repeat.
Broader and narrower express generality, not part-of; close match is weaker than exact match.
Differs from an ontology, which defines formal axioms, and from a schema, which defines data structure.

may: Propose new concepts, labels and definitions for review.
Propose candidate mappings to other schemes with a match type.
Validate a scheme for cycles, orphan concepts and duplicate labels.
Publish read-only views of an approved release.
mustNot: Treat a label or code as the identity of a concept.
Publish or approve a scheme release.
Delete or redefine a concept that objects are still classified under.
Assert an exact match where only a close match is supported.
Reassign classified objects after a scheme change.
requiresHuman: Approving a release or a namespace.
Splitting, merging or deprecating concepts in use.

considerations: Categories describing people, such as ethnicity, disability or gender, can stigmatise and need careful wording.
Classifications decide access to services, statistics and funding, so errors affect real people.
Offering labels in only one language excludes communities that use others.
affectedParties: People and groups that the categories describe
Users and systems that classify with the scheme

items: A scheme has a namespace, a set of concepts with identifiers, labels, definitions, hierarchical relations and versioned releases.
Often confused with an ontology, a code list, a glossary and a classification binding.
Breaking changes that orphan classified records.
Wrong mappings that merge distinct concepts.
Offensive or outdated terms remaining in use.
